Human history begins with a state of original hostility and conflict, a struggle for existence showing ingratitude toward the Creator.
Giving humans freedom, even "the freedom to kill oneself," removes (rightly removes) responsibility for the world's evils from God's shoulders.

Prajapati (the Creator) intervened for the benefit of suffering humanity, established laws, and entrusted a trustworthy person, Vainya (son of Vena), to be king to enforce and respect these laws.

extraction_text: A mouse lived in a cave at the roots of a large banyan tree with many entrances and exits.

The wildcat could kill the mongoose and owl, while the mongoose and owl could kill the mouse unless the mouse received protection from the wildcat.
The mouse offered to chew through the hunter's net to free the wildcat in exchange for protection.
The wildcat agreed but secretly planned to catch the mouse once freed.
The mouse chewed slowly, avoiding the key ropes, as dawn approached, forcing the blind owl to return to its nest.
The hunter arrived, the mongoose escaped, and the mouse chewed the final rope, freeing the wildcat who climbed the tree.
The mouse returned to its hole, and the wildcat came down to thank the mouse, but the mouse wisely refused to come out.

Bharadvaja asks for details, and Bhrigu describes how the five elements emerge from emptiness to earth, each evolving from the former.

Bhrigu describes the duties of the four castes.

She reminded him that he would soon meet the gods of Dharma, Time, Death, and Yama.
Soon, these gods approached the Brahmin, wanting him to go to their heavenly abode as the fruit of his recitation.

characters: Gods of Dharma, Time, Death, Yama

extraction_text: While the Brahmin was serving these guests from other worlds, King Ikshvaku appeared before him.

The Brahmin said he had entered the path of renunciation and would no longer accept gifts, but he would give the king a gift according to the king's wish.
The king said he wanted to obtain the merit the Brahmin had acquired through reciting the Vedas.
The Brahmin pointed out to the king that he recited the Vedas without expecting any fruit, so he couldn't determine what merit he would receive.
The king said he wouldn't accept a gift of unknown nature and again asked the Brahmin to accept his gift.
While the king and Brahmin were arguing, two poorly dressed, clumsy men appeared before them, engaged in a heated argument, and requested King Ikshvaku to arbitrate.

One named Virupa told the king: 'Vikrita gave a cow to a Brahmin. I begged him for the merit of this donation. He generously gave it to me. After obtaining this merit, I bought a pair of milk cows and gave them to someone who lived by gathering grains. Having double merit, I approached Vikrita and offered him the merit. But he refused to accept it. This is the focus of our argument.'
When the king inquired, Vikrita said he wouldn't accept anything from Virupa because Virupa didn't owe him anything.
Inspired by these two arguers, the Brahmin convinced the king to accept the fruit of his lifelong recitation.

Bhishma ended this story of the reciter, saying the king and Brahmin received after death rewards comparable to those obtained by yogis.
Yudhishthira asked Bhishma: What is the fruit of pursuing knowledge and observing Vedic rituals? How does one know the soul or self?

In his conversation with Brihaspati, Manu first distinguished between the path of action and the path of knowledge. The latter is knowledge of the self.
The individual self experiences good and bad fruits. The self in essence is imperceptible to the senses and indestructible.
Manu then pointed out the evolution of the five elements, each later one evolving from the former. The first element, space, arises from the indestructible self ('the Imperishable').
He continued that the individual self contacts the five elements, with the five senses respectively relying on the properties of the five elements.

The soul becomes unmanifest after one body disintegrates, and becomes manifest again after entering another body.
Manu then explained to Brihaspati that the self can only be 'seen' or known by someone whose mind has abandoned all passions, is in a tranquil state, and undisturbed.
